walkthroughs.body_html:
The incarnation is God becoming human in Jesus.

John 1:14 — 'The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.' Jesus is fully God and fully human.

Christians celebrate this at Christmas — the birth of Jesus to Mary, conceived by the Holy Spirit.

Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate. For Christians this was not a defeat — it was atonement.

Sin had broken the relationship between humans and God. Jesus' death pays that debt and restores the link.

Romans 5:8 — 'While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.' Good Friday remembers this sacrifice.

On the third day Jesus rose from the dead — the resurrection (Easter Sunday). 40 days later he ascended to heaven.

The resurrection proves Jesus' victory over sin and death and gives hope of eternal life.

Ephesians 2:8 — 'By grace you have been saved through faith.' Salvation is a free gift, not earned by works alone.

mcqs.q: What do orthodox Christians believe about the nature of Jesus?
options: He is fully God and fully human at the same time (the incarnation) — both natures united in one person, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon.
Jesus was half God and half human.
The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.

mcqs.q: What do Christians mean by resurrection, and how does it differ from reincarnation?
options: Resurrection is the once-for-all bodily raising to eternal life at the end of time (modelled on Christ's resurrection); reincarnation is the soul's repeated rebirth into new bodies. They are distinct doctrines from different religious traditions.
Resurrection and reincarnation are basically the same idea of life after death.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
Christians believe everyone is reincarnated until they accept Jesus.

mcqs.q: What is the doctrine of the Trinity?
options: Christians believe everyone is reincarnated until they accept Jesus.
The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
Christians believe in three different gods.
God is one being existing in three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) — distinct in person but united in essence; Christians remain monotheistic.
